text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure for this token game: each member starts with 20 tokens, keeping tokens privately gives me 1 point but costs each other member 0.75, while putting tokens in the group account gives me 0.75 with no cost to others. I'm setting up the formula to calculate total points based on my private holdings versus group contributions.

Since keeping a token yields 1 point individually versus only 0.75 from the group, keeping dominates as the individual rational choice even though it's collectively worse — if everyone keeps everything, each ends up with just 20 points, whereas full cooperation yields 60 points each, showing the classic tension between individual and group incentives.

Reconsidering: contributing a token costs me 0.25 net but creates 2.25 in value for others, so total welfare rises by 2 per token contributed — a real efficiency gain even though it's individually costly. That makes a moderate, partially cooperative choice worth weighing rather than pure defection.
